items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] What’s that, I just read a quote from Andre Previn... [INTERVIEWEE] Well in harmony and in theory it’s really much easier to write for four voices or five voices.

ctx.x: the great Duke Ellington is taking time out to show me some voicings. Other band leaders have been striving, trying to figure out what did he do there, how did he voice that.

What’s that, I just read a quote from Andre Previn, who said a thousand musicians can get together and play a chord that Stan Kenton wrote and all the arrangers know how to do that. And Duke Ellington writes something for three instruments and they play it and I don’t know what it is.

Well in harmony and in theory it’s really much easier to write for four voices or five voices. But to write for three voices and two voices, because he had three trombone players, and those three trombone players sounded like five or six of them sometimes. But I found after working with the band I discovered in a very short time that you could have Ellington’s band play an arrangement, and then have another choice band, maybe like a New York band or an L.A. band, all great musicians, playing the same chart, but…
